content: Contagious shooting, also referred to as mass reflexive response, is a phenomenon where gunfire spreads among officers who believe they or their colleagues are facing a threat. This reaction can propagate in a manner similar to the spread of germs, laughter, or fear. Incidents: 2006 (Sean Bell Incident): Five officers discharged a total of 50 rounds at Sean Bell, an unarmed man leaving his bachelor party in New York. One detective alone fired 31 shots, reloading his weapon during the incident. 2006 (Pit Bull Incident): In the Bronx, New York, three officers fired 26 shots at a pit bull that had bitten a chunk out of an officer’s leg. 2005 (Brian Allen Incident): Eight officers in Queens, New York, fired 43 shots at Brian Allen, an armed man, resulting in his death. 2005 (Carl Williams Incident): In Los Angeles County, California, six sheriff's deputies fired over 50 shots into a car driven by Carl Williams, a suspected drunk driver, after his vehicle rammed a police car during a chase. One deputy reloaded his weapon during the event. 2004 (Winston Hayes Incident): Deputies fired 120 shots at Winston Hayes, a 44-year-old drug suspect, after his SUV lurched forward and struck a police car. Hayes survived with four bullet wounds. However, one deputy was struck, 11 bullets hit patrol cars, and 11 others struck five homes in the neighborhood. One bullet tore a hole in a homeowner's hat. 1999 (Amadou Diallo Incident): Four officers fired 41 shots at Amadou Diallo, an unarmed man, in the Bronx, New York, on February 4, 1999. 1998 (Daniel Reyes Incident): New Jersey State Police fired 11 shots at Daniel Reyes and three other basketball players in their car in April. Usage and Expert Commentary: In a 2006 incident in New York, where five officers fired 50 rounds at a man, police experts suggested that contagious shooting might have been a contributing factor. David Mamet, quoted in the Baltimore Sun on May 24, 2006, explained, If one fires, the rest fire. It is called contagious shooting. People start shooting; they don’t even know why. The New York Times on March 26, 1999, reported that some law enforcement officials acknowledged the possibility that only one or two officers perceived a danger, while others began firing simply because their colleagues had started shooting. This phenomenon is recognized in law enforcement as contagious shooting. Thomas Reppetto, head of the Citizens Crime Commission, noted that the term contagious shooting was used during the 1960s riots. In such scenarios, an officer might fire at what they believed to be a sniper, prompting other officers to follow suit.
